newsitem.title: UK: Global business travellers suffer mental strain.
newsitem.headline: Global business travellers suffer mental strain.

text.p: Business travellers, especially men, are much more likely to suffer psychological problems than colleagues who do not travel, U.S. researchers reported on Wednesday.

Dr Bernard Liese and colleagues at the World Bank studied insurance claims made by business travellers and found those who were sent overseas were twice as likely to make claims for psychological disorders.
Those who made two or three overseas trips a year were three times as likely to make such claims, the researchers found in a study reported by the journal Occupational and Environmental Medicine.
"It surprised us. We didn't expect it," said Lorraine Nagy, a health analyst who worked on the study.

Nagy said her group at first set out to analyse general health claims for 5,000 staff at the World Bank and found, as they expected, more insurance claims for infections, back injuries and other physical consequences of travel.
"But then out pops at us increased rates of stress-related psychological disease," Nagy said in a telephone interview.
They also found that women did better. While men who travelled made 80 percent more overall health claims than men who did not, women travellers only made 18 percent more.

Men were twice as likely to claim for infectious diseases, while women were only 50 percent as likely. And while men made up to triple the psychological claims, women were only twice as likely to make them.

Nagy said she had no explanation. "It could be how women work, their ability to communicate their concerns, maybe to communicate better," she said. "Maybe these differences exist elsewhere with men and women."
But Liese suggested: "Maybe the explanation is that they (women) are just a bit sturdier."
Liese said he at first thought jet lag was to blame, but he discussed the findings with employee focus groups and found many other factors.
The World Bank employees, like many business travellers, were very dedicated to their work in general -- and work done while travelling was even more intense.
"There are many more pressures than you tend to admit," he said.
Nagy said the travellers worked very hard while on the road. "They work through the weekend, they work though the night."
Then they come home -- and face domestic challenges.
"They first have to deal with what has gone on in the meantime because no one has replaced them," Liese said. Much of this was dull paperwork -- in contrast to the excitement and status of travel.

"If you are coming back from Asia and you go through some time zones you are always a bit grumpy," Liese said. "And then my wife has all the letters and the bills. And then she expects me to be loving husband."
Nagy said such stories were always told -- but had never been analysed.
Liese said the group looked to see if any similar studies had been done, and found almost nothing. He said he hoped other big organisations would follow up with their own research.
Liese and Nagy said very small and inexpensive adjustments could help employees be less of a drain on insurance companies and on their own offices.

"They want to be able to make a decision. If it is up to them to take a day off before they come back to the office, knowing that is out there and knowing the choice is there could go very far to helping them," Nagy said.
